blocks.text:
Design the core bidding engine behind an online auction platform like eBay. A bidder does not manually type "I bid one dollar more than the last person" over and over. Instead, they enter the maximum they are willing to pay, and the system automatically bids on their behalf, just enough to stay in the lead, up to that maximum, whenever someone else places a competing bid. To keep a bidder from winning by sniping in the final second, a bid placed very close to the scheduled end time automatically extends the auction, giving everyone a fair chance to respond.

  • Actors: Bidder (places a maximum proxy bid), AuctionService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: proxy (automatic) bidding with correct price computation, a minimum bid increment, and anti-sniping deadline extension.

The distinguishing mechanic is a real proxy-bidding algorithm: the system never reveals a bidder's true maximum, only bids the minimum necessary over the previous leader's maximum, combined with a dynamic deadline that extends itself whenever a late bid threatens to end the auction unfairly.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Place a proxy bid: a bidder submits the maximum amount they are willing to pay for an item.
Automatic price computation: the displayed current price is always just enough to beat the previous leader's maximum, never revealing anyone's true ceiling.
Minimum bid increment: a new bid must clear the current price by at least a minimum increment to be accepted.
Anti-sniping extension: a bid placed within a short window of the scheduled end time automatically pushes the end time later.
Auction closure: once the end time passes with no further extension-triggering bids, the auction ends and the current leader wins at the current price.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many concurrent auctions and bidders must not require touching existing bidding logic.
Extensibility: a different minimum-increment scheme (scaling with price range) should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: increment rules, notification, and id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: recomputing the leader and displayed price on a new bid is O(1).
Thread safety: two bids on the same auction submitted concurrently must resolve to one consistent leader and price.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: Can a bidder raise their own existing maximum bid later, or is one proxy bid per bidder per auction final?
Should the minimum increment scale with the current price, or stay fixed regardless of how high the bidding goes?
How close to the end time should a bid trigger an extension, and by how much should the deadline extend?
Is there a hidden reserve price the item must meet to actually sell, separate from the starting price?
Should a bidder be notified in real time when they have been outbid, or is that outside this design's scope?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: Each bidder places at most one proxy bid per auction in this design; a bidder who is already the current leader attempting to bid again is rejected, rather than supporting raising one's own existing maximum, which is noted as a follow-up.
The minimum increment is a fixed value (5) for this design, via a pluggable strategy that could scale with price in a more advanced version.
A bid within 5 time units of the scheduled end time extends the auction by 10 time units; these are configurable constants.
There is no separate hidden reserve price in this design; the starting price is the only floor.
Real-time outbid notifications to a bidder are handled through the same Observer mechanism used for every other lifecycle event, not a separate subsystem.

blocks.text: The design centers on three core entities:

items: Item: the thing being sold, with a starting price.
Auction: tracks the current leader, the leader's true maximum, the currently displayed price, and the end time.
Bid: one bidder's submitted maximum for a specific auction.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: An item maps to exactly one auction; an auction receives many bids over time; each bid belongs to one bidder

items: Item to Auction is one-to-one.
Auction to Bid is one-to-many.
Bid to Bidder is many-to-one.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep increment rules, notification, and id creation decoupled from the core service.

Why needed: how large a minimum increment is required above the current price is a policy decision that could plausibly scale with price range (a real auction site often requires a larger increment on a thousand-dollar item than a ten-dollar one) independently of the core proxy-bidding algorithm.

metadata.alt: BidIncrementStrategy interface with FixedIncrementStrategy returning a constant minimum increment

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a new increment scheme (tiered by price range) is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to AuctionService. What it solves: it isolates a business rule likely to change from stable bidding mechanics.

Why needed: a bid being placed, a bid being rejected, an auction being extended, and an auction ending are all events a real auction platform would want to react to (outbid alerts, closing-soon notifications).

metadata.alt: AuctionObserver interface notified by AuctionService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: AuctionService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core bidding workflow from side effects.
Why needed: auction and bid id generation should not be scattered across calling code.

metadata.alt: AuctionIdFactory generating sequential A and B prefixed ids

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: every auction and bid is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Item: attributes itemId, title, startingPrice; responsibility: describe what is being sold.
Auction: attributes auctionId, itemId, sellerId, highestBidderId, highestMax, currentPrice, endTime, status; responsibility: track the live state of one auction.
Bid: attributes bidId, auctionId, bidderId, maxAmount; responsibility: represent one submitted proxy bid.
AuctionIdFactory: methods nextAuctionId, nextBidId; responsibility: generate sequential, correctly-prefixed ids.
AuctionService: the orchestrator; responsibility: validate bids, run the proxy-bidding price algorithm, extend deadlines, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: BidIncrementStrategy and AuctionObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: BidIncrementStrategy: minIncrement(currentPrice): returns the minimum amount a new bid must clear the current price by.
AuctionObserver: onBidPlaced / onBidRejected / onAuctionExtended / onAuctionEnded: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: The proxy-bidding workflow, alongside its rejection branches, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Check the auction is active and the bid clears the minimum, recompute the leader and price, then extend the deadline if the bid arrived within the anti snipe window

items: Happy path, new leader: bid → active, clears minimum → new max beats the current leader's max → new bidder leads, price set just above the old leader's ceiling.
Happy path, leader unchanged: bid → active, clears minimum → new max does not beat the leader's max → leader stays, price rises just above the new challenger's ceiling.
Rejection paths: bid → auction already ended → rejected, or → does not clear the minimum → rejected.
Extension path: any accepted bid arriving within the anti-snipe window of the end time → deadline pushed later.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: placeBid(auctionId, bidderId, maxAmount, currentTime): validates and applies a proxy bid, recomputing the leader and price, or throws if disallowed.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: BidNotAllowedException: the bid does not clear the required minimum, or the bidder is already the current leader.
AuctionEndedException: a bid is placed after the auction's end time has passed.
InvalidAuctionException: an unknown auction id.

blocks.text: The critical race is two bids on the same auction submitted at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to bid on the same auction; synchronization ensures one bid is processed first and the other resolves against the freshly updated price

blocks.text: Synchronizing the read-compare-update step per auction ensures the leader and price are always updated atomically, so two concurrent bids can never both believe they are the leader.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A tiered increment strategy (a larger minimum increment on higher-priced items) is a new BidIncrementStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (real-time outbid alerts, closing-soon push notifications) is a new AuctionObserver implementation.
Supporting a bidder raising their own existing maximum can be added by relaxing the same-bidder rejection and handling that case as an update rather than a new competing bid.
A hidden reserve price can be layered on by adding a check at auction-end time comparing the final price against the reserve.
Single Responsibility: Auction tracks live bidding state, BidIncrementStrategy decides the minimum increment, AuctionObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new increment or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to AuctionService.
Liskov Substitution: any BidIncrementStrategy or AuctionObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: AuctionObserver exposes only the four lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: AuctionService depends on the BidIncrementStrategy and AuctionObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
The very first bid on an auction sets the leader and true maximum, but the displayed price stays at the starting price until a second bidder creates real competition.
A new challenger's max exactly equals the current leader's max: the existing leader keeps the lead, since they were there first, and the price is capped at the leader's own true maximum.
A bid arriving exactly at the anti-snipe window boundary is treated as within the window, extending the deadline, using an inclusive comparison.
Multiple bids in a row each fall within the anti-snipe window, extending the deadline more than once, which is expected behavior, not a bug.
placeBid: O(1) for the validity checks, the leader-and-price recomputation, and the anti-snipe extension check.
Space: O(auctions + bids) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

items: An index on Bid(auctionId) supports building a full bid history for a given auction.
The Auction row itself holds the live, frequently-updated leader and price fields, kept separate from the append-only Bid history.
Support a bidder raising their own existing maximum bid rather than rejecting a second bid from the current leader outright.
Add a hidden reserve price that must be met for the item to actually sell.
Support a tiered increment strategy scaling with the current price range.
In a distributed deployment, move auction-state locking to a database-level row lock or a distributed lock rather than in-process synchronization.

blocks.text: AuctionStatus, Item, Auction, Bid and AuctionIdFactory:

codes.python:
from enum import Enum

# Lifecycle status of a single auction.
class AuctionStatus(Enum):
    ACTIVE = "ACTIVE"  # still accepting bids
    ENDED = "ENDED"    # closed, no further bids accepted

# The item being sold, with its starting price.
class Item:
    def __init__(self, item_id, title, starting_price):
        self.item_id = item_id            # unique id
        self.title = title                  # display title
        self.starting_price = starting_price  # the floor, shown before any real competition exists

# Tracks the live bidding state of one auction.
class Auction:
    def __init__(self, auction_id, item_id, seller_id, starting_price, end_time):
        self.auction_id = auction_id      # unique id, e.g. A1
        self.item_id = item_id              # which item this sells
        self.seller_id = seller_id            # who is selling it
        self.highest_bidder_id = None           # nobody has bid yet
        self.highest_max = 0.0                    # no true maximum yet
        self.current_price = starting_price         # starts at the item's floor
        self.end_time = end_time                      # store initial deadline
        self.status = AuctionStatus.ACTIVE              # starts active

# One bidder's submitted maximum for a specific auction.
class Bid:
    def __init__(self, bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, max_amount):
        self.bid_id = bid_id            # unique id, e.g. B1
        self.auction_id = auction_id      # which auction this targets
        self.bidder_id = bidder_id          # who placed it
        self.max_amount = max_amount          # the true maximum, never revealed to other bidders

# Creates sequential, correctly-prefixed ids for auctions and bids.
class AuctionIdFactory:
    def __init__(self):
        self.auction_counter = 0  # running id counter for auctions
        self.bid_counter = 0        # running id counter for bids

    def next_auction_id(self):
        self.auction_counter += 1  # bump id counter
        return f"A{self.auction_counter}"  # e.g. A1

    def next_bid_id(self):
        self.bid_counter += 1  # bump id counter
        return f"B{self.bid_counter}"  # e.g. B1

blocks.text: AuctionService, including the proxy-bidding price algorithm and anti-sniping extension:

codes.python:
# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class BidNotAllowedException(Exception): pass
class AuctionEndedException(Exception): pass
class InvalidAuctionException(Exception): pass

# The core orchestrator tying every piece together.
class AuctionService:
    ANTI_SNIPE_WINDOW = 5     # bids within this many time units of the end trigger an extension
    ANTI_SNIPE_EXTENSION = 10  # how far the deadline pushes out when triggered

    def __init__(self, increment_strategy):
        self.auctions = {}                # auctionId -> Auction
        self.increment_strategy = increment_strategy  # pluggable increment policy
        self.observers = []                  # listeners

    def add_auction(self, auction):
        self.auctions[auction.auction_id] = auction  # register an auction

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def place_bid(self, auction_id, bidder_id, max_amount, current_time, factory):
        auction = self.auctions.get(auction_id)  # look up auction
        if auction is None:
            raise InvalidAuctionException(f"Unknown auction: {auction_id}")
        if current_time >= auction.end_time:  # auction already over
            raise AuctionEndedException(f"Auction {auction_id} has already ended")
        required_minimum = auction.current_price + self.increment_strategy.min_increment(auction.current_price)  # must clear this
        if max_amount < required_minimum:  # bid does not clear the minimum
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_bid_rejected(bidder_id, auction_id, "Bid too low")  # notify
            raise BidNotAllowedException(f"Bid must be at least {required_minimum}")
        if bidder_id == auction.highest_bidder_id:  # already the current leader
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_bid_rejected(bidder_id, auction_id, "Already the highest bidder")  # notify
            raise BidNotAllowedException(f"{bidder_id} is already the highest bidder")
        bid_id = factory.next_bid_id()  # build id
        bid = Bid(bid_id, auction_id, bidder_id, max_amount)  # build the bid record
        if auction.highest_bidder_id is None:  # this is the very first bid
            auction.highest_bidder_id = bidder_id  # this bidder leads
            auction.highest_max = max_amount          # their true maximum
            # current_price stays at the starting price, since there is no competitor to beat yet
        elif max_amount > auction.highest_max:  # new challenger beats the old leader
            old_highest_max = auction.highest_max  # remember the old ceiling
            new_price = min(max_amount, old_highest_max + self.increment_strategy.min_increment(auction.current_price))  # just enough to beat it
            auction.highest_bidder_id = bidder_id  # new bidder takes the lead
            auction.highest_max = max_amount          # their true maximum
            auction.current_price = new_price           # update displayed price
        else:  # old leader stays ahead
            new_price = min(auction.highest_max, max_amount + self.increment_strategy.min_increment(auction.current_price))  # just enough to beat the challenger
            auction.current_price = new_price  # leader keeps lead at a higher price
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_bid_placed(bid, auction.current_price)  # notify
        if auction.end_time-current_time <= self.ANTI_SNIPE_WINDOW:  # this bid arrived late
            new_end_time = current_time + self.ANTI_SNIPE_EXTENSION  # push the deadline out
            auction.end_time = new_end_time  # apply the extension
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_auction_extended(auction_id, new_end_time)  # notify
        return bid  # hand back to caller

items: Why never reveal a bidder's true maximum to anyone, including the losing bidders? Because doing so would let a competitor bid exactly one increment above it deliberately, defeating the entire purpose of proxy bidding, which is to let a bidder state their true ceiling once without needing to babysit the auction.

Why extend the deadline rather than simply rejecting bids placed too close to the end? Because rejecting late bids would let a sniper deliberately time their bid to land just after that cutoff and never be challenged at all; extending the deadline instead gives every other bidder a genuine chance to respond.

How would you support a bidder raising their own maximum bid? Detect that the incoming bidderId already equals the current leader and, instead of rejecting outright, update their stored maximum if it is higher, without changing who currently leads or the displayed price unless a competing bid now exceeds the new maximum.

Proxy bidding vs simple highest-bid-wins: proxy bidding lets a bidder participate once and trust the system to bid minimally on their behalf, a much better experience than requiring them to manually respond to every competing bid, at the cost of a genuinely more complex pricing algorithm to implement correctly.

Anti-sniping extension vs a hard fixed deadline: a hard deadline is simpler to reason about, but rewards bidders who snipe in the final second at the expense of everyone who bid earlier and in good faith; a self-extending deadline is fairer at the cost of an auction's actual end time being unpredictable in advance.

Fixed increment vs tiered increment: a fixed increment is simple and predictable, at the cost of feeling either too small on an expensive item or too large on a cheap one; a tiered strategy fixes that at the cost of a slightly more complex rule to communicate to users.
Persist items, auctions, and bids in a relational database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.

Emit bid/extension/ended events to a message queue so downstream systems (outbid notifications, closing-soon alerts, payment processing) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to placeBid so retried network requests cannot double-apply the same bid.
Expose metrics on how often auctions get extended, which can reveal whether the anti-snipe window is calibrated appropriately for how bidders actually behave.
